facts.F4: The husband has significant health issues, including stage IV cancer of the oesophagus, and is currently in remission.
facts.F5: The husband originally issued proceedings for divorce in 2011, but the parties reconciled and the petition was withdrawn.
facts.F6: The wife undertook to pay the husband HK$10,000 per month for his financial support and entered into a non-molestation undertaking as part of the reconciliation.
facts.F7: The wife failed to honor her promise and undertaking to pay the husband HK$10,000 a month, causing financial stringency to him.
facts.F8: The wife sent the husband numerous abusive and degrading text messages while he was hospitalized in Taiwan for cancer treatment.
facts.F9: The husband and wife continued to live under the same roof, but in strained circumstances, after he returned from hospital treatment.
facts.F10: The husband's hospitalization was in Taiwan.
facts.F11: The husband and wife had no sexual relationship after he returned from hospital treatment.
facts.F12: There was no resumption of cohabitation between the parties after the husband's discharge from hospital.

facts.F1: The applicants are children of Yam Wai Cho, who married Madam Lai Wan Chee in 1917 according to Chinese rites and custom.
facts.F2: Madam Lai Wan Chee died in 1940, and Mr. Yam Wai Cho married Madam Chan Lai Fong in 1941, also according to Chinese rites and custom.
facts.F3: The applicants were raised by Madam Chan Lai Fong, who never had any children of her own.
facts.F4: After the applicants got married, they continued to support and maintain Madam Chan Lai Fong financially until her death in 2001.
facts.F5: The applicants were treated as Madam Chan Lai Fong's children, and she was treated as their mother, within the family and in dealings with people outside the family.
facts.F6: The legislative intention behind the repeal of section 2(2)(b) of the Intestates' Estates Ordinance in 1995 was to bring the law in line with current day community expectations and remedy various legal inconsistencies and anomalies.
facts.F7: In Chinese customary law, the concept of 'tin fong' (田房 or 填房) refers to a second wife who marries into a family and 'fills up' the vacancy left behind by the former wife, becoming the mother of all children born by the previous wife.

facts.F2: The Official Receiver filed an application on 4th July 2003 to object to the automatic discharge of the Bankrupt.

facts.F4: The Bankrupt claimed to have sold the horse to Mr. Lau Kit Ming for $150,000, but the Official Receiver disputed the validity of the sale.
facts.F5: The horse was transferred to Mr. Lau on 10 October 1999, and later transferred back to the joint names of Mr. Lau and the Bankrupt since April 2000.
facts.F6: The Official Receiver requested the Bankrupt to cooperate in selling the horse, but the Bankrupt refused, claiming the horse was no longer his asset.
facts.F7: The Official Receiver sought to put the horse for tender sale in August 2002, but the Bankrupt did not cooperate.
facts.F8: The Bankrupt alleged that he was under pressure from Mr. Lau and was forced to sell the horse unwillingly.
facts.F9: The Law Reform Commission's Report on Bankruptcy explained the rationale and purpose of automatic discharge of a bankrupt.
facts.F10: The Bankrupt was under pressure from Mr. Lau at the time of the sale.

lawsuit_type: Bankruptcy proceedings - objection to automatic discharge

requested_remedy: The plaintiffs claimed for damages arising from the death of the deceased caused by the collapse of an awning erected by the 4th defendant, including loss of dependency, loss of accumulated wealth, bereavement, and funeral expenses.
parties: Plaintiff: CHU WO HEUNG and PAK YUEN SAU, the Administratrices of the estate of YUEN FOOK WAH, deceased

Defendant: HUI LAI WA formerly trading as LUNG FUNG SUPER SEASONAL FRUIT, WONG SHUET YING and LIU WAI KEUNG, INCORPORATED OWNERS OF LUNG FUNG GARDEN, WONG PUN WAI, HANG YICK PROPERTIES MANAGEMENT LTD, LO MANG LUN, CHAN WAI CHUN NELLY and CHOW SIU LIN

facts.F1: YUEN FOOK WAH, a resident owner of a flat in Lung Fung Garden, Fanling, was killed on 3 August 1994 when an awning erected by the 4th defendant collapsed.
facts.F2: The awning was a flimsy and dangerous structure with a metal pipe that penetrated into the chest of YUEN FOOK WAH, killing him.
facts.F3: YUEN FOOK WAH left behind a wife, CHU WO HEUNG, and two children aged 2 and 1 at the time of his death.
facts.F4: YUEN FOOK WAH was born in China in 1954 and had been working in Hong Kong for 18 years before his death.
facts.F5: He had been driving professionally as a driver of goods vehicles between China and Hong Kong since 1989.
facts.F6: YUEN FOOK WAH and his wife lived in Dongguan and later moved to Hong Kong.
facts.F7: YUEN FOOK WAH's assets at the time of his death were estimated to be worth $3.7 million.
facts.F8: The Inland Revenue Department assessed additional tax of $477,077 on YUEN FOOK WAH's income for 1990-1995.
facts.F9: The Cheuk Hung Log Book was used as a contemporaneous document to determine the deceased's trucking income.
facts.F10: The deceased received gifts from friends.
